lead: A pure substance in a single phase has its state fixed by any two independent properties (the state postulate). Every other property is then a function of two variables, z = z(x, y), and the calculus of such functions gives the three tools of property relations: the exact differential and its test, the reciprocity relation and the cyclic relation. With them a slope that cannot be measured is written in terms of slopes that can, which is the whole purpose of thermodynamic relations. This chapter sets out the three tools and tries each one on an ideal gas.
prereq: You need: partial derivatives from calculus, and the ideal-gas equation pv = RT.

sections.h3: Two-variable functions and the total differential

blocks.text: For a simple compressible substance any property z can be written as z = z(x, y), where x and y are two independent properties; for example p = p(T, v). A small change in both gives the total differential
The subscript names the property held fixed. M = (∂z/∂x)<sub>y</sub> and N = (∂z/∂y)<sub>x</sub> are the two slopes. For p = RT/v, M = (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = R/v and N = (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = −RT/v².

A partial derivative is a slope along a line on the property surface: (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> is the slope of a constant-volume line on a p–T diagram, and (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> is the slope of an isotherm on a p–v diagram.

sections.h3: The exact differential and its test

blocks.text: M dx + N dy is exact when it is the differential of some function z. Then the two mixed second derivatives of z are equal, ∂²z/∂y∂x = ∂²z/∂x∂y, which gives the test:

blocks.where: If the test holds, the integral of dz between two states is the same on every path and the integral round any cycle is zero: z is a property (a point function). If it fails, the quantity depends on the path.

blocks.text: Properties such as p, v, T, u, h and s have exact differentials. Heat and work do not: they are path functions, which is why many books write δq and δw. For an ideal gas on a reversible path, δq = c<sub>v</sub>dT + p dv = c<sub>v</sub>dT + (RT/v)dv. Here ∂(c<sub>v</sub>)/∂v = 0 but ∂(RT/v)/∂T = R/v, so δq is not exact. Divide by T: ds = (c<sub>v</sub>/T)dT + (R/v)dv, and now both cross-derivatives are zero, so ds is exact. 1/T is the integrating factor that turns heat into the property entropy. Figure 4.3.1 shows this with two paths between the same two states.
Take three properties x, y and z linked by one equation of state, so each is a function of the other two. The two relations follow in five steps:

items: Write x = x(y, z): dx = (∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>dy + (∂x/∂z)<sub>y</sub>dz. Write y = y(x, z): dy = (∂y/∂x)<sub>z</sub>dx + (∂y/∂z)<sub>x</sub>dz.
Put the second into the first: dx = (∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>(∂y/∂x)<sub>z</sub>dx + [(∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>(∂y/∂z)<sub>x</sub> + (∂x/∂z)<sub>y</sub>]dz.
x and z are independent, so the coefficient of dx must be 1 and the coefficient of dz must be 0.
Coefficient of dx: (∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>(∂y/∂x)<sub>z</sub> = 1, the reciprocity relation.
Coefficient of dz: (∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub>(∂y/∂z)<sub>x</sub> = −(∂x/∂z)<sub>y</sub>; with reciprocity on the right this is the cyclic relation.

blocks.where: Reciprocity: a slope and its inverse, taken with the same property held fixed.

blocks.text: Cyclic relation: x, y, z go round in the numerators and denominators, and each subscript is the third property. The product is −1, not +1, because the three slopes are taken along three different lines on the surface, so the ∂ symbols do not cancel like fractions.

With p, v and T the cyclic relation gives the most used result of this kind: (∂p/∂T)v = −(∂v/∂T)p/(∂v/∂p)T. The pressure rise of a liquid heated in a sealed vessel, which is hard to measure, follows from two easy measurements, one at constant pressure and one at constant temperature (see Expansivity, compressibility, Mayer relation and Joule-Thomson coefficient).

examples.question: Check the cyclic relation (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub>(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>(∂T/∂p)<sub>v</sub> = −1 for air as an ideal gas at 300 K and 100 kPa, with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Also check reciprocity for (∂T/∂p)<sub>v</sub>.
examples.answer: The product of the three slopes is −1.000, as the cyclic relation says, and (∂T/∂p)<sub>v</sub> = 3.000 K/kPa is the reciprocal of (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = 0.3333 kPa/K.

examples.question: 1 kg of air (ideal gas, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/(kg·K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) goes reversibly from state 1 (300 K, 0.861 m³/kg) to state 2 (600 K, 1.722 m³/kg). Path A: heat at constant volume to 600 K, then expand isothermally at 600 K. Path B: expand isothermally at 300 K, then heat at constant volume to 600 K. Find the heat and the entropy change on each path, and say which of δq and ds is exact.
steps: Constant-volume heating from 300 K to 600 K: q = c<sub>v</sub>ΔT = 0.718 × 300 = 215.4 kJ/kg and Δs = c<sub>v</sub>ln 2 = 0.718 × 0.6931 = 0.4977 kJ/(kg·K).
Isothermal doubling of volume at temperature T: q = RT·ln 2 and Δs = R·ln 2 = 0.287 × 0.6931 = 0.1989 kJ/(kg·K).
Test of δq = c<sub>v</sub>dT + (RT/v)dv: ∂(c<sub>v</sub>)/∂v = 0 but ∂(RT/v)/∂T = R/v, so δq is not exact. Test of ds = (c<sub>v</sub>/T)dT + (R/v)dv: both cross-derivatives are 0, so ds is exact.
examples.answer: The heat differs, 334.8 kJ/kg on path A and 275.1 kJ/kg on path B, but the entropy change is 0.6966 kJ/(kg·K) on both. Heat is a path function; entropy is a property.

traps: Writing the cyclic relation with +1. The product of the three slopes is −1.
Cancelling ∂ symbols like fractions across different subscripts. Only two slopes with the same subscript obey reciprocity.
Testing exactness with the wrong derivative: M is differentiated with respect to y, the other variable, not x.
Calling q exact because the end states are fixed. The second worked example gives 334.8 and 275.1 kJ/kg between the same two states.

quiz.q: State the condition for M dx + N dy to be an exact differential.
quiz.a: (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub>: the two mixed second derivatives are equal.

quiz.q: Write the reciprocity and cyclic relations for p, v and T.
Why is the differential of a property exact while δw is not?
quiz.a: A property depends only on the state, so its change between two states does not depend on the path and its mixed derivatives are equal. Work is the area under the path on a p–v diagram, so it changes with the path and no function w(state) exists.

quiz.q: Test dz = (2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy for exactness and find z.
quiz.a: ∂M/∂y = 2x and ∂N/∂x = 2x, so it is exact. z = x²y + 3x + 2y² + constant (check: ∂z/∂x = 2xy + 3, ∂z/∂y = x² + 4y).

quiz.q: For a van der Waals gas, p = RT/(v − b) − a/v². Find (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and (∂T/∂p)<sub>v</sub>.
A student writes (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub>(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> by cancelling ∂v. Test it for air at 300 K and 100 kPa.
quiz.a: Left side: (−116.1) × 0.00287 = −0.3333 kPa/K. The true (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> is +0.3333 kPa/K. The sign is wrong: the cyclic relation carries a minus sign.

beyond: Jacobians give a quick, mechanical way to convert any partial derivative of p, v, T and s into measurable ones; Bridgman's tables list them all. Carathéodory built a statement of the second law on the existence of an integrating factor for δq, the same 1/T that appears in this chapter. Search next: Jacobian method in thermodynamics, Bridgman tables, Carathéodory principle.

figure.caption: Two reversible paths for 1 kg of air from state 1 (300 K, 0.861 m³/kg) to state 2 (600 K, 1.722 m³/kg): the heat is 334.8 kJ/kg on one path and 275.1 kJ/kg on the other, but the entropy change is 0.6966 kJ/(kg·K) on both, because ds is exact and δq is not.
